artiest/donovan.text:
Donovan Leitch was born in Glasgow in 1946 and grew up in Hatfield, in England. As a child he contracted polio, which left him with a limp. Folk songs were sung a great deal at home, and he began playing the guitar at fourteen. He abandoned art college, travelled around as a busker and learned the fingerpicking technique in the St Albans folk scene. In early 1965 he made his breakthrough with appearances on the television programme Ready Steady Go! and his first single, Catch the Wind.

The British press at first saw him as an answer to Bob Dylan, but his songs were lighter and more optimistic. With the producer Mickie Most he found a sound of his own, in which folk came together with pop, psychedelia and jazz. The album Sunshine Superman (1966) features sitar and congas. The title track reached number 1 in America in 1966, followed by Mellow Yellow. Jennifer Juniper, Hurdy Gurdy Man (1968) and Atlantis (1969) were among the songs that came after. Musicians who would later form Led Zeppelin, such as Jimmy Page and John Paul Jones, played on his records.

Donovan became the singer of the flower-power era. He was friends with Joan Baez, Brian Jones and The Beatles, and, like The Beatles, travelled to India to study with the Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. In 1968 he taught John Lennon a fingerpicking style that Lennon used in Dear Prudence and Julia. After 1969 his success declined, and after the rise of punk critics found his hippie image old-fashioned. In 1996 he made the album Sutras with the producer Rick Rubin. In 2012 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/donovan.listen: Listen to Sunshine Superman and hear how Donovan blends his folk background with the new psychedelic pop of 1966. Then compare it with Dear Prudence by The Beatles and listen for the fingerpicking style that Lennon learned from Donovan.

artiest/dorian-electra.text:
Dorian Electra was born in 1992 in Houston, Texas, into a Jewish family. Their father was known in the city as the Rockstar Realtor, and their mother is an artist and jewellery designer. At secondary school Electra founded a philosophy club, and from 2010 to 2014 studied at Shimer College in Chicago, a school where the great books are read. Electra is genderfluid and uses the pronoun they.

In 2010 Electra attracted attention with the music video I'm in Love with Friedrich Hayek, a eulogy to the philosophy of the Austrian economist. Videos such as Roll with the Flow and We Got it 4 Cheap followed, and in 2014 What Mary Didn't Know, based on a philosophical thought experiment. In 2015 came Forever Young: A Love Song to Ray Kurzweil. From 2016 Electra made a series for Refinery29 on the history of feminism and queer culture, with titles such as 2000 Years of Drag. In 2017 the single Jackpot was released and Electra took part in Femmebot by Charli XCX. The debut album Flamboyant came out in 2019, followed by My Agenda in 2020 and Fanfare in 2023.

Electra is known for an idiosyncratic style, a queer aesthetic and experimental pop. Music, fashion and philosophy merge into one another, which fits the hyperpop and internet culture of the 2010s. They turn ideas from science and history into danceable pop music with a wink.
artiest/dorian-electra.listen: Listen to Flamboyant and notice the electronic sounds, the thick bass and the playful, exaggerated way of singing. What do the lyrics tell you about how Electra looks at masculinity and style?

artiest/dorothy-dandridge.text:
Dorothy Dandridge was an American singer and actress, born in 1922 in Cleveland, Ohio. Her mother Ruby devised a singing and dancing act for her two daughters, The Wonder Children, and the sisters toured the southern United States for years. In the 1930s the family moved to Hollywood. By 1934 the group was called The Dandridge Sisters and was appearing in nightclubs such as the Cotton Club and at the Apollo Theater in New York.

Dorothy appeared in films as a child. In 1941 she sang and danced in Sun Valley Serenade, in a number with the Nicholas Brothers, and she took part in Duke Ellington's revue Jump for Joy. In the 1940s she sang in films with Count Basie and Louis Armstrong and made ten Soundies, short music films for jukeboxes with a screen. Her nightclub career took off remarkably from 1951, when she performed at the Mocambo in West Hollywood. In 1954 she played the lead in Carmen Jones, a film version of Oscar Hammerstein's musical that transfers Bizet's opera to an African American setting. Her singing voice in that film was dubbed by Marilyn Horne. She became the first African American actress to be nominated for an Oscar for Best Actress.

Porgy and Bess followed in 1959. Because of the limited roles that Hollywood offered Black actresses, her film career remained small. She died in 1965, aged 42. Her career shows how music, film and the nightclub world overlapped in the America of her day.
artiest/dorothy-dandridge.listen: Listen to a recording of Dorothy Dandridge from a film or nightclub and notice her light, controlled voice. Can you hear how she makes every word count without forcing?

artiest/doug-watkins.text:
Douglas Watkins was born in Detroit in 1934 and became one of the most sought-after bassists in hard bop. He was one of the original members of the Jazz Messengers and afterwards played in Horace Silver's quintet. He also worked as a freelancer with, among others, Gene Ammons, Kenny Burrell, Donald Byrd, Art Farmer, Jackie McLean, Hank Mobley, Lee Morgan, Sonny Rollins and Phil Woods. According to Horace Silver's autobiography, Watkins and Silver left Art Blakey's band because they were tired of the police checks to which the group was exposed because of other members' drug problems.

His best-known recording is the one on Sonny Rollins's 1956 album Saxophone Colossus, on which, at the age of twenty-two, he plays alongside Max Roach and Tommy Flanagan. In 1961 Charles Mingus hired him for the bass part when Mingus himself sat down at the piano for a while, which led to the albums Oh Yeah and Tonight at Noon.

As a bandleader he made only two albums: Watkins at Large for Transition and Soulnik for New Jazz. For the latter, recorded in 1960 with Yusef Lateef, he played cello, an instrument he had only begun playing a few days earlier. In 1962 he was killed in a car accident near Holbrook, Arizona, at the age of 27. His name therefore appears mainly on other people's records, as the steady, driving bass beneath the hard bop of the 1950s.
artiest/doug-watkins.listen: Listen to Saxophone Colossus by Sonny Rollins and try to follow Doug Watkins's bass. Can you hear how he plays a steady line that Rollins and Max Roach can move over?

artiest/dr-dre.text:
Dr. Dre was born Andre Romell Young in 1965 in Compton, a suburb of Los Angeles. He is a rapper, but above all a producer. With his slow, rich beats he defined the sound of West Coast hip hop in the 1990s, and he discovered and mentored artists such as Snoop Dogg and Eminem.

He began in 1984 as a DJ in the World Class Wreckin' Cru and in 1987 co-founded N.W.A. That group brought gangsta rap to a wide audience, with the album Straight Outta Compton (1988). In 1991 Dre founded the label Death Row Records with Suge Knight. His first solo album The Chronic (1992) laid the foundations for G-funk: slow funk grooves with synthesizers and plenty of space in the mix. The single Nuthin' but a "G" Thang, featuring the young rapper Snoop Doggy Dogg, reached number 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1993. Dre then produced Snoop's debut Doggystyle (1993) and, with 2Pac, California Love (1995). In 1996 he left Death Row and started his own label, Aftermath, where he signed Eminem in 1998. His second album 2001 (1999) opened with the single Still D.R.E., built on a stark keyboard melody by Scott Storch.

Dre also became an entrepreneur. He co-founded the headphone brand Beats, which Apple acquired in 2014. In 2000, like Metallica, he brought a lawsuit against Napster. In 2022 he appeared at the Super Bowl halftime show with Snoop Dogg, Eminem, Mary J. Blige and Kendrick Lamar.
artiest/dr-dre.listen: Nuthin' but a "G" Thang is built on a sample of I Want'a Do Something Freaky to You by the soul singer Leon Haywood. Listen to how Dre slows that soul groove down and leaves space, so that Snoop Doggy Dogg can rap over it in a relaxed, almost lazy way.

artiest/dr-dre-en-roger-troutman.text:
Roger Troutman was born in 1951 in Hamilton, Ohio, the fourth of nine children. With his brothers he founded Zapp, who were discovered in 1979 by George Clinton and signed to his label Uncle Jam Records. A year later Troutman signed with Bootsy Collins to Warner Bros. The debut album Zapp produced More Bounce to the Ounce, which reached number two on the Billboard Soul Singles chart at the end of 1980. Up to 1985 came gold albums such as Zapp II and Zapp III and top hits on the R&B chart, such as Dance Floor and Computer Love. In 1993 Zapp & Roger: All the Greatest Hits was released. Troutman died in 1999.

His trademark was the talk box, a device connected to an instrument, usually a keyboard or guitar, that makes the instrument sound as if it is talking. He used a specially built Electro-Harmonix Golden Throat, via a Minimoog and later a Yamaha DX100. Zapp helped to push funk forward, and West Coast hip hop sampled their music extensively.

Dr. Dre, known from N.W.A and West Coast hip hop, made California Love with him in 1995. On that track Troutman sings through the talk box, so that the chorus line sounds in an electronic, robotic voice. It is an example of how the funk of Zapp was given a new lease of life in the hip hop of the 1990s. Troutman regularly collaborated with hip hop artists in those years.
artiest/dr-dre-en-roger-troutman.listen: Listen to California Love and notice the voice from the talk box, which sounds like a singing robot. How does that electronic voice fit with the heavy bass and the rap?

artiest/dr-feelgood.text:
Dr. Feelgood were an English pub rock band from Canvey Island in Essex. Guitarist Wilko Johnson, singer Lee Brilleaux, bassist John B. Sparks and drummer John Martin formed the band in 1971. The name comes from a 1962 record by the blues pianist Willie Perryman, also known as Piano Red, which was released under the name Dr. Feel-Good. Around 1973 they were one of the most popular groups on the London pub circuit. In 1974 they recorded their debut album Down by the Jetty.

The breakthrough album was the live album Stupidity from 1976, which reached number one in England and was the group's only record to do so. In the United States the Ramones played in May 1976 as the support act for their performances at the Bottom Line in New York. After Sneakin' Suspicion in 1977 Johnson left the band after conflicts with Brilleaux, and Gypie Mayo took his place. With Mayo the group had their only top-ten single in 1979, Milk and Alcohol. Brilleaux kept the group going until he died of lymph node cancer in 1994.

The sound was raw British rhythm and blues, with Johnson's choppy guitar style as its hallmark and a bare, fast rhythm section. It was music for packed halls and pubs, without slick production. Dr. Feelgood were therefore regarded as a forerunner of punk, a line that Julien Temple's 2009 film Oil City Confidential also follows.
artiest/dr-feelgood.listen: Listen to Milk and Alcohol and notice the tight, dry guitar riff and the raw voice of Lee Brilleaux. Can you hear how the song stays free of frills?

artiest/dr-luke.text:
Dr. Luke is the stage name of Łukasz Gottwald, an American musician, songwriter and producer, born in 1973 in Providence, Rhode Island. He spent much of his youth in New York, wanted to become a drummer and at thirteen began on his sister's guitar. He studied for two years at the Manhattan School of Music and from 1996 to 2007 was lead guitarist in the house band of the television programme Saturday Night Live.

Through a meeting with the Swedish producer Max Martin he found his way into pop production. In 2004 he wrote and produced Since U Been Gone for Kelly Clarkson together with Martin. Who Knew for Pink, Girlfriend for Avril Lavigne and I Kissed a Girl for Katy Perry followed, among others. He worked on Britney Spears's Femme Fatale from 2011 and produced Part of Me and Wide Awake for Perry. He founded the labels Kemosabe Records and later Amigo Records, and in 2022 produced Super Freaky Girl for Nicki Minaj. In 2014 a series of lawsuits with Kesha began, which was settled out of court in 2023.

His work is built on clear choruses, loud guitars and electronic rhythms. In 2010 Billboard named him producer and songwriter of the year. Dr. Luke represents the glossy, layered pop production of the 2000s and 2010s, in which producers became just as important as the singers.
artiest/dr-luke.listen: Listen to Since U Been Gone by Kelly Clarkson and notice how the guitars and the electronic beat together build up the chorus. Can you hear how the verse begins quietly and the chorus then bursts open?

artiest/drake.text:
Aubrey Drake Graham, known as Drake, was born in 1986 in Toronto. His father is an African American drummer from Memphis, his mother a Canadian teacher. At fifteen he landed the role of Jimmy Brooks in the Canadian teen series Degrassi: The Next Generation. Alongside acting he began making music. In 2006 he released the mixtape Room for Improvement himself and in 2009 came So Far Gone, available as a free download via his blog, with the singles Best I Ever Had and Successful. He then signed to Young Money Entertainment.

His debut album Thank Me Later appeared in 2010 and went straight to the top of the Billboard 200. Take Care in 2011 and Nothing Was the Same in 2013 built his name further. Views in 2016, Scorpion in 2018, Certified Lover Boy in 2021 and Her Loss and Honestly, Nevermind in 2022 followed. He founded the label OVO Sound and became an ambassador for the Toronto Raptors.

Drake is seen as someone who brought R&B feeling into hip hop by rapping and singing on the same track. His lyrics often deal with doubt, love and fame, over dark, spacious beats. He is one of the best-selling artists in the world and showed that a Canadian rapper could define the hip hop of the 2010s, in a scene that had long been mainly American.
artiest/drake.listen: Listen to Best I Ever Had and notice how he switches between rapping and singing. Can you hear how the soft, melodic beat keeps the track calm?

artiest/dreams-come-true.text:
Dreams Come True is a Japanese pop group founded in 1988 by the singer Miwa Yoshida, bassist Masato Nakamura and keyboardist Takahiro Nishikawa. In Japan the band is known simply as DCT or Dorikamu. Their first album, Dreams Come True, was released in 1989 and sold more than a million copies in Japan. The fifth album, The Swinging Star from 1992, was the first Japanese album to sell more than three million copies.

Nakamura also composed the music for the Sega Mega Drive games Sonic the Hedgehog from 1991 and Sonic the Hedgehog 2 from 1992. For the second game their song Sweet Sweet Sweet was used as the ending theme. In 1993 they recorded Winter Song for the Japanese version of the film Sleepless in Seattle. Yoshida appeared on the cover of Time in 1996. In 1997 they signed to Virgin Music America in order to break into the United States, but their English-language album Sing or Die from 1998 flopped. Nishikawa left the group in 2002. Later they wrote songs for Disney, including the Japanese theme song for Inside Out.

The group plays cheerful, bright pop with a striking, powerful singing voice, melodic bass lines and plenty of keyboards. The band is important above all as an example of the enormous home-market success of J-pop in the 1990s, independent of the Western charts.
artiest/dreams-come-true.listen: Listen to Sweet Sweet Sweet and notice Masato Nakamura's playful bass line and Miwa Yoshida's bright voice. Can you hear how the song stays cheerful, even in the chorus?

artiest/duane-eddy.text:
Duane Eddy was an American guitarist, born in 1938 in Corning, New York. He started playing the guitar at the age of five, after hearing the singing cowboy Gene Autry. The family moved to Arizona, where he formed a duo with his friend Jimmy Delbridge. In Phoenix he met the disc jockey and songwriter Lee Hazlewood, who began producing his records. Eddy was not happy with his singing voice and therefore played the melody on the low strings of his Gretsch guitar, with a deep, reverberating tone that became known as twang.

In 1958 Movin' n' Groovin' reached the American chart. He borrowed the riff from Chuck Berry, and a few years later the Beach Boys took it over again for Surfin' U.S.A. Rebel-'Rouser, with a saxophone by Gil Bernal, followed, then Peter Gunn, Cannonball, Shazam and Because They're Young. His debut album Have 'Twangy' Guitar Will Travel stayed in the album chart for 82 weeks. His band, with saxophonists Steve Douglas and Jim Horn and keyboardist Larry Knechtel, later supplied musicians to Phil Spector's Wrecking Crew. Eddy also acted in films, and in the 1970s produced for Phil Everly and Waylon Jennings.

His instrumental guitar sound, bare, low and heavily reverberant, was one of the first recognisable guitar sounds of rock and roll. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1994 and died in 2024.
artiest/duane-eddy.listen: Listen to Peter Gunn and notice the low, reverberant guitar line that carries the melody. Can you hear how the guitar sings without needing a voice?

artiest/dudu-pukwana.text: The alto saxophonist Dudu Pukwana grew up in Port Elizabeth and began as a pianist. In Chris McGregor's Blue Notes he became one of the most striking voices: his saxophone sounded sharp, joyful and full of kwela and mbaqanga. In 1964 he left for Europe with the group and settled in London. There he played in Brotherhood of Breath and led groups of his own such as Spear and Zila. That blend is easy to hear on Diamond Express (1975). He also played with British jazz and rock musicians. He died in London in 1990.
artiest/dudu-pukwana.listen: Listen to the sharp, dancing saxophone above township rhythms.

artiest/duke-ellington.text: Edward Kennedy 'Duke' Ellington grew up in Washington, where he learned James P. Johnson's Carolina Shout from a piano roll, and came to New York in 1923. From 1927 to 1931 he led the Cotton Club orchestra, which became famous through the radio. Ellington did not write for a hired orchestra but for the sound of his own musicians, such as Bubber Miley's growling trumpet and Johnny Hodges's alto saxophone. He led his orchestra for almost fifty years. He wrote more than a thousand pieces, from short numbers to suites and sacred concerts, often together with Billy Strayhorn. His performance at the Newport Jazz Festival in 1956 won him a new audience. He died in New York in 1974.
artiest/duke-ellington.listen: Pay attention to the tone colours: muted trumpets and saxophones in unusual combinations.

artiest/duke-ellington-en-his-washington.text:
The Washingtonians was the band name under which Duke Ellington became known in the early 1920s. Ellington was born in 1899 in Washington, D.C., and grew up with piano-playing parents. He wrote his first composition in 1914, Soda Fountain Rag, while still unable to read music. From 1917 he put together groups to play at dances. In 1919 he met the drummer Sonny Greer, and together they went to New York, where Ellington ended up in Harlem.

There the group played in 1923 under the name Elmer Snowden and his Black Sox Orchestra. It was an ensemble of seven men, including the trumpeter Bubber Miley, which in September 1923 began a four-year residency at the Hollywood Club, later the Kentucky Club. They called themselves The Washingtonians. When Snowden left in early 1924, Ellington took over the leadership. That year he made eight records. The orchestra grew to ten players and found a sound of its own in Ellington's arrangements, the rhythms of Harlem, the growling trombones and the high trumpets.

This was the foundation on which Ellington went on to build. In 1927 the orchestra gained a permanent place at the Cotton Club in Harlem, with weekly radio broadcasts. Bubber Miley, with his growl trumpet, gave the group a hotter sound, in the style that was then called Jungle Style. The Washingtonians are thus the starting point of the career of one of the most important composers in jazz.
artiest/duke-ellington-en-his-washington.listen: Listen to Duke Ellington's East St. Louis Toodle-Oo from 1926 and notice Bubber Miley's growling trumpet. Can you hear how the band sounds hotter here than an ordinary dance band?

artiest/duke-ellington-orchestra.text:
The Duke Ellington Orchestra was the big band of the pianist, composer and bandleader Duke Ellington from Washington. From the 1920s the band played in New York, including at the Cotton Club in Harlem. Ellington wrote his pieces for the musicians he had to hand. He knew exactly how each soloist sounded and used those tone colours as a painter uses paint. In this way the band became one of the most important orchestras of the swing era.

In 1939 the composer and arranger Billy Strayhorn joined the band. He wrote Take the A Train, which was recorded in 1941 and grew into the orchestra's signature tune. Ellington's son Mercer also wrote pieces for the band in those years. After Duke Ellington's death in 1974 Mercer took over the leadership. He toured Europe with the orchestra and won a Grammy in 1988 with the album Digital Duke. After him his son Paul and grandson Edward kept the name alive.
artiest/duke-ellington-orchestra.listen: Listen to Take the A Train and follow the form: the same section twice, then a different middle section and then the return of the opening. Also notice how the brass and the saxophones alternate with each other.

artiest/duke-reid.text:
Arthur Duke Reid was a Jamaican producer, disc jockey and record boss, born in 1915. He was a police officer for ten years, and afterwards took over the family shop with his wife Lucille, the Treasure Isle Grocery and Liquor Store in Bond Street in Kingston. In 1953 he started a sound system, a mobile open-air disco, which quickly became the most popular in Kingston. He was known as The Trojan, and also presented a radio programme, Treasure Isle Time. Reid himself was a lover of jazz and blues.

In the late 1950s he began making records, first in other people's studios and later in a studio of his own above the shop. He had several labels, of which Treasure Isle became the most important. In the 1960s he dominated the Jamaican music scene with ska and rocksteady. He at first found ska too simple and too focused on the drums, but still made a long string of hits in it. A fierce rivalry with Coxsone Dodd and his Studio One ran throughout the 1960s, including in the battle between their sound systems. At toasting competitions Reid appeared in an ermine cape with a golden crown, revolvers and a shotgun.

In the 1970s Rastafarian roots reggae emerged, which he banned from his studio. As a result Coxsone Dodd gained more room. When he became seriously ill, he sold Treasure Isle to Sonia Pottinger. He died in 1975. Reid showed how a producer who owned a sound system could define the sound of an island, and in 2007 he was posthumously awarded a Jamaican honour.
artiest/duke-reid.listen: Listen to a ska or rocksteady recording on the Treasure Isle label and notice the rhythm of the guitar on the second and fourth beats. Can you hear how the bass carries the song and how warm the horns sound?

artiest/duncan-laurence.text:
Duncan Laurence is the stage name of Duncan de Moor, a Dutch singer and songwriter, born in 1994 in Spijkenisse and raised in Hellevoetsluis. As a teenager he began writing songs, partly as an escape from bullying. He studied at the Rock Academy in Tilburg and played in school bands, including his own group The Slick and Suited, formed in 2013. He then took part in the fifth season of The Voice of Holland, with Ilse DeLange as his coach. He was eliminated in the semi-final. He also co-wrote Closer, a song by the Korean duo TVXQ.

In January 2019 he was internally selected to represent the Netherlands at the Eurovision Song Contest in Tel Aviv. His song Arcade was released in March of that year. He was the big favourite and won, giving the Netherlands its first win since 1975. In 2020 Arcade became a hit on TikTok, and in January 2021 it was the most-streamed Eurovision song on Spotify. His first album is called Small Town Boy, from 2020, followed by Skyboy in 2023. At the 2021 Eurovision Song Contest in Rotterdam he opened the first semi-final with Feel Something.

Laurence sings softly and sensitively, accompanied by piano and little embellishment. His song about a lost love remains simply built and only late on grows into a grand chorus. He shows that a Eurovision winner can reach a much larger audience through streaming than just the television audience of a single evening.
artiest/duncan-laurence.listen: Listen to Arcade and notice how the song begins with just piano and voice. Can you hear how the tension grows step by step towards the chorus?

artiest/duran-duran.text:
Duran Duran are an English pop band from Birmingham. The childhood friends Nick Rhodes and John Taylor started the group in 1978 and named it after a character in the science-fiction film Barbarella. After many changes, the settled line-up was in place in 1980: singer Simon Le Bon, keyboardist Rhodes, bassist John Taylor, guitarist Andy Taylor and drummer Roger Taylor. The band was the house band of the Rum Runner club, whose owners became their managers.

The debut album Duran Duran was released in 1981, with Planet Earth as the first hit and then Girls on Film. The sound combined synthesizers with a danceable bass, rock guitar and Le Bon's singing. Duran Duran belonged to the New Romantics, the British scene of flamboyant clothing and make-up. Rio (1982) included Hungry Like the Wolf, Save a Prayer and Rio, with videos that the director Russell Mulcahy shot as short films in exotic locations. Seven and the Ragged Tiger (1983) yielded The Reflex, and in 1985 came the Bond theme A View to a Kill.

Duran Duran was one of the first bands to see the music video as an important medium. When MTV began in the United States in 1981, the group benefited fully and became a pioneer of the new British invasion of America. Around 1984 the frenzy around the band was compared with that around The Beatles. After line-up changes the group scored again in 1993 with Ordinary World. In 2022 Duran Duran were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/duran-duran.listen: Listen to Planet Earth and notice the combination of synthesizers, a tight, danceable bass line and sharp guitar. Hear how the song sounds at once like a rock band and like a record for the dance floor.

artiest/dustin-o-halloran.text:
Dustin O'Halloran is an American composer and pianist, born in 1971 in Phoenix and raised in Hawaii and Los Angeles. While studying art in Santa Monica he met the singer Sara Lov. In 1998 they started the indie rock band Dévics together. When the group signed to Bella Union in 2001, they moved to Italy. In 2004 his first solo record, Piano Solos, was released, and in 2006 Piano Solos, Vol. 2 followed. Later solo albums include Lumiere from 2011, with Peter Broderick and Adam Wiltzie, and in 2019 he signed to Deutsche Grammophon.

Besides his solo records he forms the ambient duo A Winged Victory for the Sullen with Adam Wiltzie, who made albums such as Atomos from 2014, The Undivided Five from 2019 and Invisible Cities from 2021. In 2015 they played at the Royal Albert Hall during the BBC Proms. O'Halloran also wrote film music, including for Sofia Coppola's Marie Antoinette from 2006 and for Like Crazy from 2011. In 2015 he won an Emmy for the theme tune of the series Transparent. Together with Hauschka he made the music for the film Lion, which received, among other honours, an Oscar nomination.

His music is restrained and calm, often for piano alone or with strings and electronics, and resembles a kind of small film image. He belongs to the modern classical movement in which piano music, ambient and film music flow into one another.
artiest/dustin-o-halloran.listen: Listen to a piece from Piano Solos and notice how slow and simple the melody is. Can you hear the silence between the notes, and how it lets the piece breathe?

artiest/dusty-springfield.text:
Dusty Springfield was born Mary O'Brien in 1939 in West Hampstead in London, into a family of Irish parents who loved music. At home she listened to Gershwin, Cole Porter, Count Basie, Duke Ellington and Glenn Miller. She first sang in folk clubs with her brother Dion, later known as Tom Springfield. In 1958 she joined the Lana Sisters and in 1960 she formed the folk-pop trio The Springfields with her brother and Tim Feild. In 1963 she left the group to go solo.

In the 1960s she had great success in Britain with singles such as I Only Want to Be With You, I Just Don't Know What to Do with Myself, the best known of her many Burt Bacharach and Hal David covers, In the Middle of Nowhere and Some of Your Lovin'. Her albums from that period include A Girl Called Dusty from 1964, Ev'rything's Coming Up Dusty and The Look of Love from 1967. She presented Ready Steady Go! on British television and from 1966 to 1969 had her own programmes on the BBC and ITV. In 1966 she topped the Melody Maker polls.

Dusty sang with a dark, distinctive mezzo-soprano and performed blue-eyed soul, pop ballads, chanson, country and jazz. Her voice was warm and dramatic and sometimes sounded almost whispered. She was one of the first British female singers to have success with American soul, and so showed that British pop and Black American music could strengthen each other. She died in 1999.
artiest/dusty-springfield.listen: Listen to I Only Want to Be With You and notice how her voice sounds both powerful and sensitive. Can you hear how she breaks free of the accompaniment in the chorus?

artiest/dutch-swing-college-band.text:
The Dutch Swing College Band is a traditional Dixieland band founded on 5 May 1945 by the clarinettist and saxophonist Peter Schilperoort. The group was very successful in the Netherlands and soon gained an international audience too. The line-up changed over the years, with, among others, Huub Janssen on drums, Kees van Dorser on trumpet, Dim Kesber on saxophone, Jan Morks on clarinet, Oscar Klein on trumpet and Dick Kaart on trombone. Schilperoort led the band for more than forty-five years, although in 1955 he took a five-year break for a career as an engineer. On 1 January 1960 he officially returned.

In 1976 the band provided the interval act of the Eurovision Song Contest, broadcast live from The Hague. After Schilperoort's death in 1990, Bob Kaper, a member since 1967, took over the leadership. The band still tours a great deal, especially in Europe and Scandinavia, and still records.

The music is Dixieland: the jazz style from New Orleans, in which trumpet, clarinet and trombone each play a line of their own at the same time above a driving rhythm section of banjo or guitar, bass and drums. The Dutch Swing College Band showed that this music could have a large audience outside America too. The Dutch jazz audience of the post-war years found a group of its own in the band.
artiest/dutch-swing-college-band.listen: Listen to Way Down Yonder in New Orleans and notice how trumpet, clarinet and trombone weave in and out of each other. Can you follow the three horns separately while the rhythm section carries on?

artiest/e-t-mensah.text: E.T. Mensah from Accra was a trumpeter who, shortly after the Second World War, became the leader of The Tempos, a dance orchestra that blended swing with Ghanaian rhythms and calypso. In this way he shaped dance-band highlife and earned the nickname King of Highlife. The band toured all over West Africa. At Ghana's independence in 1957 his Ghana Freedom was heard, and he played together with Louis Armstrong.
artiest/e-t-mensah.listen: Listen to All for You: horns as in a swing band, but beneath them a skipping Ghanaian rhythm on the drums.

artiest/e-t-mensah-en-the-tempos.text:
Emmanuel Tettey Mensah was born in 1919 in Ussher Town in Accra, then still the Gold Coast, and was later known as the King of Highlife. At twelve he learned to play the flute in the school band, and in 1932 he played piccolo and flute in the Accra Orchestra, an orchestra of schoolchildren. Together with his older brother Yebuah, who led a dance orchestra, he formed the Accra Rhythmic Orchestra, which won the Lambeth Walk Dance Competition in 1939.

The first Tempos came into being in 1946 as a jam session group of European soldiers in Accra, who played for army parties and in a club in the city. Gradually the Europeans were replaced by African musicians, until it was an entirely African band, led by Joe Kelly and then by Guy Warren. Mensah joined the band in 1947. Soon afterwards the group broke up and was re-formed with Mensah as leader. The Tempos toured widely in West Africa. One of his best-known compositions is Ghana Freedom, a song associated with Ghana's independence that celebrates the struggle and reward of the people of the Gold Coast.

Highlife is the dance music of West Africa, in which local rhythms and guitar lines are combined with brass and the dance-orchestra sounds of Western swing. In the 1960s the style fell into decline, but Mensah remained active. In 1983 he made the successful album Highlife Giants of Africa Vol. 1 with the Nigerian trumpeter Victor Abimbola Olaiya. He died in 1996.
artiest/e-t-mensah-en-the-tempos.listen: Listen to Queen's Visit and notice the horns, the light, danceable rhythms and the swinging mood. Which elements sound African and which come from Western dance music?

artiest/eagles.text:
The Eagles are an American rock band from Los Angeles, formed in 1971. Glenn Frey, Don Henley, Bernie Leadon and Randy Meisner first played in the backing band of the singer Linda Ronstadt. During a tour with her, Frey and Henley decided to start a band of their own. David Geffen signed them to his new label Asylum. The debut Eagles was released in 1972, recorded in England with the producer Glyn Johns. He was impressed by their multi-part singing and turned them into a country rock band with high, clear harmonies.

The first single was Take It Easy, which Frey wrote together with his neighbour Jackson Browne. Desperado (1973), On the Border (1974) and One of These Nights (1975) followed. Henley and Frey wrote more and more together and became the leaders of the band. They wanted to move away from country rock and towards harder rock. With the arrival of the guitarists Don Felder and Joe Walsh the band sounded more solid. On Hotel California (1976) it all came together: polished rock with country roots, sharp guitars and lyrics about the dark side of life in California. The title track and New Kid in Town were number 1 hits.

After The Long Run (1979) the band broke up in 1980, but in 1994 it reformed. The Eagles are one of the best-selling bands in the world. Their mix of rock, country and harmony singing defined the sound of American radio in the 1970s. In 1998 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/eagles.listen: Listen to Take It Easy from 1972. Notice the acoustic guitars, the banjo and above all the high multi-part singing in the chorus, in which you can hear the country in their rock.

artiest/earl-hines.text: The pianist Earl Hines came from near Pittsburgh and played in Chicago from 1925. In 1928 he recorded the Hot Five records with Louis Armstrong; their duet Weather Bird is regarded as a high point. With his right hand Hines played lines in octaves that sounded like a trumpet, so that they cut through a band. This is why people spoke of his 'trumpet style'. He interrupted the steady stride accompaniment of the left hand and played with greater rhythmic freedom. From 1928 he led a big band at the Grand Terrace in Chicago for more than ten years. In the early 1940s Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and Sarah Vaughan played in his orchestra. In the 1960s he enjoyed a second career as a soloist.
artiest/earl-hines.listen: Listen for the right hand in octaves: a piano trying to sound like a trumpet.

artiest/earl-scruggs.text:
Earl Scruggs was born in 1924 in Flint Hill, in Cleveland County, North Carolina. His father died when he was four. The whole family played music, and Earl was already working at the banjo so young that he first had to lay the instrument on the floor beside him. Around the age of ten, while playing the tune Reuben, he discovered that he was picking with three fingers instead of two. From that moment he practised every spare minute.

In 1945 he joined Bill Monroe's Blue Grass Boys, and his playing was an immediate sensation. In 1948 he left, as did the singer and guitarist Lester Flatt. Together they formed the duo Flatt and Scruggs. Their instrumental Foggy Mountain Breakdown, recorded in 1949, became a lasting hit and found a new audience when it was heard in the 1967 film Bonnie and Clyde. In 1962 they recorded The Ballad of Jed Clampett, the theme tune of the television series The Beverly Hillbillies, which reached number 1 on the Billboard chart. In 1969 they split up, because Scruggs wanted to sound more modern and Flatt held on to tradition.

The Scruggs style is fast and rhythmic. With picks on thumb, index finger and middle finger he plucks individual strings in a fixed pattern, with the melody continuing to sound between the notes. As a result the banjo became a solo instrument instead of an accompanist in the background. That way of playing became a hallmark of the whole of bluegrass. Scruggs died in Nashville in 2012.
artiest/earl-scruggs.listen: Listen to Foggy Mountain Breakdown by Flatt and Scruggs. Notice the stream of fast banjo notes: the melody is hidden in it, while the other fingers keep playing notes around it.

artiest/earth-wind-en-fire.text:
Earth, Wind & Fire began in 1969 in Chicago. Maurice White, who had worked as a session drummer at Chess Records and played in Ramsey Lewis's trio, wrote songs and advertising music there with two friends. As The Salty Peppers they had a minor hit with La La Time. White moved to Los Angeles, brought in his younger brother Verdine as bassist and gave the group a new name, taken from the elements in his horoscope. The first albums appeared in 1971, and the band also played on the soundtrack of the film Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song.

In 1972 White put together a new, younger line-up, with, among others, the singer Philip Bailey and the keyboardist Larry Dunn, and the group moved to Columbia. With Head to the Sky (1973) and Open Our Eyes (1974) their success grew. The album That's the Way of the World (1975) reached number 1, as did the single Shining Star. With that Earth, Wind & Fire became the first Black act to top the American album and singles charts at the same time. The live album Gratitude (1975) followed, and the group stayed at the top for years.

The music blends funk and soul with jazz, disco, Latin American rhythms and African influences. Its hallmarks are the powerful horn section, the kalimba, an African thumb piano, and the contrast between Maurice White's tenor voice and Philip Bailey's falsetto. On stage the band gave exuberant shows. Rolling Stone wrote that Earth, Wind & Fire changed the sound of Black popular music. The group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/earth-wind-en-fire.listen: Listen to Shining Star and notice how the horns play short, fierce stabs above a tight funk groove. Also hear how the vocals and the horns alternate with each other.

artiest/eberhard-weber.text:
Eberhard Weber is a German double bassist and composer, born in 1940 in Stuttgart. His father was a music teacher, so he received a classical training from an early age. He began on the cello at six and at sixteen, at secondary school, he took up the double bass, because his music teacher was looking for someone to play bass and he volunteered. At the amateur jazz festival in Düsseldorf he met the pianist Wolfgang Dauner, with whom he collaborated for years, from mainstream jazz to jazz rock and avant-garde experiments.

Weber began recording in the early 1960s. His first record under his own name, The Colours of Chloë, was released in 1973 on ECM. Thirteen albums under his own name followed, all on ECM. He also played in Spectrum with Dave Pike and Volker Kriegel, but left the group because he found its direction too rock-oriented. He was one of the first to use the solid-body electric upright bass, to which he added a fifth string. At ECM he worked with Gary Burton, Ralph Towner, Pat Metheny and Jan Garbarek, with whom he made ten recordings between 1978 and 1998. Alongside his music he worked for years as a television and theatre director.

Weber's compositions combine chamber jazz, European classical music, minimalism and ambient, and are regarded as typical of the ECM sound. His bass has a recognisable tone and phrasing, often singing and with a great deal of space. He showed that the bass can also be a leading melodic voice.
artiest/eberhard-weber.listen: Listen to The Colours of Chloë and notice the long, singing notes of the bass and the space between the sounds. What atmosphere is created, and how much do you hear besides the bass?

artiest/ed-blackwell.text:
Ed Blackwell was an American jazz drummer, born in 1929 in New Orleans. He grew up in a family with many musical traditions and with connections in the city's record business. He learned to read music and the basics of drumming from Wilbur Hogan, played in his school's drum band and only began on a drum kit at nineteen, when he got his first paid gig. In 1949 he played in the Jonson Brothers Band, with jump blues, rhythm and blues and shuffle. In 1951 he moved to Los Angeles, where he got to know Ornette Coleman.

His early style came from the second line rhythms of New Orleans and from the bebop of Kenny Clarke and Max Roach. Around 1960 he became a member of Ornette Coleman's quartet, after taking Billy Higgins's place during a residency at the Five Spot Café in New York. That was the period of the free jazz with which he is most closely associated. Later he played in the group Old and New Dreams, after which the 1979 album is named, and made records of his own, such as Tune In from 1969 and El Corazón from 1982. Transit from 1987 and Crystal Fire from 1992 belong there too. He died in 1992.

Even in free jazz Blackwell kept his playing structured. He used recurring motifs, which makes his drumming sound almost song-like. In this way he brought the rhythms of New Orleans into the avant-garde, and showed that free jazz and tradition are not separate from each other.
artiest/ed-blackwell.listen: Listen to a recording of Ed Blackwell with Ornette Coleman and follow only the drums. Can you hear how the rhythm sometimes almost becomes a melody, even though the tempo is not fixed?

artiest/ed-sheeran.text:
Ed Sheeran is an English singer-songwriter, born in 1991 in Halifax, West Yorkshire, and raised in Framlingham in Suffolk. His parents worked in the art world. As a child he sang in a church choir, learned to play the guitar at eleven and was already writing songs. At thirteen he released a first collection himself, Spinning Man. In 2008 he moved to London, where he played in small venues. Through YouTube and the video channel SB.TV his audience grew, and the rapper Example took him on tour.

In 2011 he released the EP No.5 Collaborations Project himself, with grime artists such as Wiley and Ghetts, which climbed high in the iTunes chart without a label or promotion. He then signed to Asylum Records. His debut album + from 2011 topped the British album chart, with The A Team as the breakthrough. × from 2014 included Thinking Out Loud. The album ÷ from 2017 became the best-selling album of that year, with Shape of You and Castle on the Hill. After that came, among others, No.6 Collaborations Project, = in 2021 and − in 2023. By his own account, as reported in the source, he has sold 200 million records.

Sheeran often plays alone on acoustic guitar and uses a loop station to build up layers himself. He combines folk, pop and hip hop, and sings and raps fluidly in and out of each other. He is an example of an artist who became an enormous global star through the internet and small gigs, with songs that stand on their own.
artiest/ed-sheeran.listen: Listen to The A Team and notice the acoustic guitar and the soft voice. Can you hear how the story of the song carries the track, rather than the production?

artiest/ed-townsend.text:
Ed Townsend was an American singer, songwriter and producer, born in 1929 in Fayetteville, Tennessee. His family moved to Memphis, where his father was a minister in an African Methodist church. After high school he travelled the world as a member of a church youth council, and then studied at the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff. In 1951 he joined the United States Marine Corps and served in Korea, for which he received a Purple Heart.

After his service he recorded a few singles for various labels, without success. In 1958 he took his ballad For Your Love to Capitol Records, in the hope that Nat King Cole would sing it. But the label was impressed by his voice and signed him itself. For Your Love became a doo-wop and R&B classic. After that he had no more hits himself. He did write for others, however, such as How Can I Forget for Jimmy Holiday in 1962, which Ben E. King later recorded, and he wrote and produced The Love of My Man for Theola Kilgore. His best-known contribution is that he co-wrote Let's Get It On with Marvin Gaye.

Townsend still appeared in 2000 in the PBS special Rock, Rhythm, and Doo Wop. He died in 2003. His son David Townsend was a member of the group Surface. He shows that much of soul history was made by writers and producers who were seldom in the spotlight.
artiest/ed-townsend.listen: Listen to Let's Get It On by Marvin Gaye and notice the relaxed, sensual groove and the soft voice. Can you hear how the song builds slowly, without hurry?

artiest/edda-dell-orso.text:
Edda Dell'Orso is the stage name of Edda Sabatini, an Italian singer born in 1935. She is known for her collaboration with the composer Ennio Morricone, for whom she sang wordlessly in many film scores. She is a soprano with a range of three octaves. She also worked for other Italian film composers, such as Alex Puddu, with whom she made albums in later years, including Registrazioni al Buio from 2013 and In the Eye of the Cat from 2016.

In Sergio Leone's spaghetti Westerns her voice was used as an instrument for the first time, with a new and dramatic effect. You can hear her in A Fistful of Dollars, in The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, above all in the piece The Ecstasy of Gold, and in Once Upon a Time in the West. Her voice sounds there without words, as a high, floating line above the orchestra. In the 1980s she also sang in the Italo disco group Bianca Neve, with Anne Dattner as the face of the group.

Dell'Orso's most important contribution is that she showed how a voice without words can carry a film scene. Her sound became a fixed part of the sound of the Western and of the Italian soundtracks of the 1960s. Many later film composers and artists from other styles still draw on that style of singing.
artiest/edda-dell-orso.listen: Listen to The Ecstasy of Gold from The Good, the Bad and the Ugly and notice Edda Dell'Orso's voice above the orchestra. Can you hear how she tells a story without words?

artiest/eddie-cochran.text:
Eddie Cochran was born in 1938 in Albert Lea, Minnesota. His parents came from Oklahoma, and in 1952 the family moved to Bell Gardens in California. In 1955 he formed the duo The Cochran Brothers with Hank Cochran, no relation. Cochran is important as a rock 'n' roll guitarist and as a musician who experimented in the studio with multitrack recording and overdubs. Among British rockers he became a hero after his death.

In the film The Girl Can't Help It (1956) he sang Twenty Flight Rock. Summertime Blues (1958) reached number 8 in America. C'mon Everybody, released at the end of 1958, he wrote with Jerry Capehart. Cochran sings, plays guitar and added an extra drum part himself. In England the song reached number 6 in 1959, in America number 35. Cochran could play guitar, piano, bass and drums.

In England Cochran was more popular than in America. From January to April 1960 he toured there with Gene Vincent. On 16 April their taxi crashed near Chippenham; Cochran died the next day in a hospital in Bath, aged 21. Three Steps to Heaven then became a British number 1. When the fifteen-year-old Paul McCartney met John Lennon in 1957, he played Twenty Flight Rock. Pete Townshend of The Who was strongly influenced by Cochran's guitar playing, and The Who and Blue Cheer made their own versions of Summertime Blues. In 1987 Cochran was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/eddie-cochran.listen: C'mon Everybody (1958): notice the stop-time riff. The band plays a short motif and then drops out, and in that silence Cochran sings his line. This puts all the attention on the voice.

artiest/eddie-condon.text:
Eddie Condon was an American banjo player, guitarist and bandleader, born in 1905 in Goodland, Indiana, and raised in Illinois. He began on the ukulele, switched to banjo and was already a professional musician in 1921. In the 1920s he played mainly in Chicago, with, among others, Bix Beiderbecke, Jack Teagarden and Frank Teschemacher. In 1925 he founded the Chicago Rhythm Kings together with Red McKenzie. He went to the Lincoln Gardens club to see King Oliver and his band and to learn from them.

In 1928 Condon moved to New York. There he organised jam sessions and recordings for record companies, sometimes with Louis Armstrong and Fats Waller, and he arranged mixed-race recording sessions at a time when they were still rare. From the late 1930s he often played at Nick's in Manhattan. The refined variety of Dixieland that he made there with his colleagues was nicknamed Nicksieland, although Condon himself hated the word Dixieland. From 1945 to 1967 he had a jazz club of his own in New York. In 1944 and 1945 his jazz concerts were broadcast from Town Hall. His autobiography is called We Called It Music, from 1948. He toured England in 1957 and Australia and Japan in 1964.

Condon played a four-string guitar, but never recorded a solo on it. His role lay mainly in organising, leading and bringing players together. He is the face of the Chicago style, a fiery, collective jazz in which everyone plays at once and drives the rhythm. He died in 1973.
artiest/eddie-condon.listen: Listen to a recording of Eddie Condon with his band, for example from the album At the Jazz Band Ball, and notice how the horns weave in and out of each other while the rhythm guitar keeps the tempo. Can you hear the guitar as a quiet engine beneath the whole?

artiest/eddie-harris.text:
Eddie Harris was an American jazz musician, born in 1934 in Chicago, with a Cuban father and a mother from Mississippi. He was taught by Walter Dyett at DuSable High School, like many other Chicago musicians, and later continued his studies. During his military service he played in Europe in the 7th Army Band. Afterwards he signed to Vee Jay Records. His first album there, Exodus to Jazz from 1961, contained his jazz arrangement of the theme from the film Exodus, which reached the American chart as a single.

In 1964 he moved to Columbia and a year later to Atlantic. There The In Sound, a bop album, was released in 1965. In the following years he played electric piano and the electric Varitone saxophone and made jazz with funk, which sold well in both jazz and R&B. His album The Electrifying Eddie Harris from 1967 reached number two on the R&B chart. In 1969 he played with Les McCann at the Montreux Jazz Festival, a performance that came about without rehearsal and was released as Swiss Movement, one of the best-selling jazz albums ever. His best-known compositions are Freedom Jazz Dance, which Miles Davis made famous in 1966, and Listen Here. He also devised instruments of his own, such as the reed trumpet, a trumpet with a saxophone mouthpiece.

Harris brought humour and experiment into jazz and showed that a saxophone with electronics could sound very different. He died in 1996 in Los Angeles.
artiest/eddie-harris.listen: Listen to Freedom Jazz Dance and notice the broken, jumpy melody. Can you hear how it sounds almost like a dance pattern that keeps coming back?

artiest/eddie-holland.text:
Eddie Holland was born on 30 October 1939 in Detroit. He began as a singer. In 1958 he recorded You (You You You You) for Mercury, a song that Berry Gordy had written and produced. When Gordy started Motown a year later, Holland went with him. As a singer he had minor hits there, such as Jamie in 1961, but he came to dislike performing.

He chose writing and, with his younger brother Brian Holland and Lamont Dozier, formed the team Holland-Dozier-Holland. Eddie wrote mainly the lyrics, while Brian and Dozier took care of the music and production. The trio made a large part of the music that became known as the Motown sound, with hits for Martha and the Vandellas, The Supremes, The Four Tops and The Isley Brothers. These included Nowhere to Run, Reflections and Baby I Need Your Loving. In addition, Holland wrote lyrics with the producer Norman Whitfield for The Temptations and The Marvelettes, such as Ain't Too Proud to Beg and Too Many Fish in the Sea.

In 1967 the trio left Motown after a dispute over their contract. A year later they started labels of their own, Invictus and Hot Wax, where Eddie also produced records. Holland wrote or co-wrote 143 hits in America and 80 in England. In 2019 an autobiography of the trio, Come and Get These Memories, was published.
artiest/eddie-holland.listen: Listen to Baby I Need Your Loving by The Four Tops. Notice Eddie Holland's simple, pleading lyrics and how the singer delivers them with growing urgency, supported by the backing vocals of the other group members.

artiest/eddie-lang.text:
Eddie Lang, born Salvatore Massaro, was born in 1902 in Philadelphia, the son of an Italian American instrument maker. He began on the violin at seven and grew up as a friend of the violinist Joe Venuti. In 1920 he switched to banjo and later to guitar. In the 1920s he played with Venuti and recorded with Roger Wolfe Kahn, Jean Goldkette and Frankie Trumbauer, and with the blues guitarist Lonnie Johnson, under the name Blind Willie Dunn to hide the colour of his skin and as a tribute to Blind Lemon Jefferson.

In 1929 Lang and Venuti joined Paul Whiteman's orchestra. Whiteman was impressed by how quickly Lang learned songs, although he had had little schooling and could not read music. That year Bing Crosby made his first solo records, and Lang became a friend of his and played in his accompaniment. Lang died in 1933, aged thirty, after a routine tonsillectomy from which he never woke up.

Lang is regarded as the father of jazz guitar. He made the guitar a solo instrument, as part of a band and as an accompanist to singers. He played the melody on a single string, with occasional chords, and used heavy strings and a high action so that his acoustic guitar remained audible among the other instruments. According to George Van Eps, banjo players had no choice but to switch to the guitar. George Harrison also named him as one of his favourite guitarists.
artiest/eddie-lang.listen: Listen to a duet by Eddie Lang with Joe Venuti and notice the guitar playing the melody on a single string. Can you hear how clear and soft the guitar sounds next to the violin?

artiest/eddie-sauter.text:
Eddie Sauter was an American composer and arranger of the swing era, born in 1914. He studied at Columbia University and the Juilliard School. He began as a drummer, then played trumpet professionally, including in Red Norvo's orchestra, and eventually became Norvo's regular arranger. He then wrote arrangements and compositions for Artie Shaw, Tommy Dorsey, Woody Herman and above all Benny Goodman.

From 1952 to 1958 he led the Sauter-Finegan Orchestra together with Bill Finegan, which made records such as Inside the Sound from 1952 and The Sound of the Sauter-Finegan Orchestra from 1953. Between 1957 and 1959 he succeeded Kurt Edelhagen as leader of the SWF orchestra in Baden-Baden. In 1961 he worked with the tenor saxophonist Stan Getz on the album Focus, for which, at Getz's request, he wrote a series of pieces for strings. For Getz he also wrote the film music for Mickey One from 1965, starring Warren Beatty. He made the theme tune for the third season of Night Gallery on television and orchestrated Broadway musicals such as 1776 and The Apple Tree.

Sauter was not a frontman but a writer behind the scenes. His arrangements gave a swing orchestra new colours and a sound of its own. The orchestrator Jonathan Tunick said of his work for Broadway that it was always theatrical and effective and unlike anyone else's. He died in 1981 and was inducted into the Big Band and Jazz Hall of Fame in 2003.
artiest/eddie-sauter.listen: Listen to Focus by Stan Getz and notice how Eddie Sauter's string orchestra surrounds the saxophone. Can you hear how the saxophone plays freely while the strings form a written-out background?
